title: Total mercury exposure in early pregnancy has no adverse association with scholastic ability of the offspring particularly if the mother eats fish.
ehr_evidence: we therefore used the comprehensive data collected on a population of pregnant women in the UK in 1991–2, whose total blood mercury level is available for the first half of pregnancy; blood samples were sent to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for analysis of whole blood mercury, and maternal fish consumption was obtained via a 32-week gestation food frequency questionnaire.
summary: In the ALSPAC prospective birth cohort, prenatal total blood mercury (measured in the first trimester) showed no adverse association with offspring scholastic abilities (reading, spelling, phoneme, mathematics, science) after adjustment, an effect that was conditional on maternal fish consumption.
key_findings: After adjustment there were no significant associations between prenatal total blood mercury and any of the 15 scholastic outcomes (e.g. spelling 7-year adjusted β +0.02 (−0.16, +0.20), P=0.833; word reading 7-year adjusted β +0.09 (−0.30, +0.48), P=0.646).
Scientific reasoning SY6 was weakly significant unadjusted (β +0.36 (0.26, 0.47), P<0.0001) but not after adjustment (β +0.12 (−0.00, +0.27), P=0.054).

Logistic regression for being in the lowest 15% of each score showed apparent protective effects that became non-significant after adjustment (e.g. spelling 7-year adjusted OR 0.94 (0.83, 1.08), P=0.408).

No significant associations for either fish eaters or non-fish eaters after adjustment, but significant interactions: maternal mercury was negatively associated with mathematics (SY6, SY8) and science reasoning (SY6) results when the mother did not eat fish, versus positive associations when she did.
No statistically significant sex differences (boys vs girls) were found.
captured_features: maternal whole blood total mercury (μg/L, first trimester)
maternal fish consumption (white/oily fish frequency via questionnaire)
scholastic test scores (spelling, reading, phoneme, mathematics reasoning, scientific reasoning)
maternal age, parity, maternal education, housing tenure, household crowding, stressful life events, prenatal smoking, prenatal alcohol, breastfeeding, family adversity index
age at testing, sex of child
quintile/centile categories of mercury for threshold analysis
population: ALSPAC UK cohort; women with due dates 1 April 1991–31 December 1992; offspring followed into childhood, analysis sample of 1569–2224 children tested at ages 7–13 years.
limitations: Notable attrition among children requiring clinic attendance, causing bias toward higher socioeconomic participants.
Relatively small numbers of children whose mothers did not eat fish (minimum 120–121), limiting power in the non-fish subgroup.
Single first-trimester blood measurement may not represent mercury exposure later in pregnancy.
Missing data not assumed to be at random and were not analysed.
